JSON: Name: joint_conformational_sequence_optimization Title: Joint optimization of sequence-to-structure and structure-to-sequence models for improving de novo protein folding stability design and prediction Short Hypothesis: Jointly optimizing P(sequence|structure) and P(structure|sequence) during sequence generation causes designed protein sequences to exhibit higher experimental folding stability (larger ΔG) and fewer alternative low-energy conformations than sequences produced by optimizing either objective alone. Related Work: Existing approaches to de novo protein design follow two principal paradigms: fixed-backbone sequence design using structure-conditioned models (P(sequence|structure)) and sequence-to-structure optimization using structure predictors (P(structure|sequence)). Structure-conditioned models can sample sequences compatible with a given backbone but assume the input backbone is a good representation of the global energy minimum and cannot detect or remove sequence-induced alternative conformations. Sequence-to-structure optimization (including gradient-based hallucination and energy-based methods) directly searches for sequences that maximize the predicted probability of a target fold but may not reduce absolute energy and can be trapped in local minima; structure predictors can also assign high confidence to adversarial or non-native-like sequences. Hybrid and diffusion-based generative methods broaden design diversity but do not explicitly enforce joint consistency between sequence likelihood and structure stability. Prior zero-shot scoring methods and single-model confidence filters partially correlate with experimental stability but fail to distinguish sequence-driven instabilities within the same fold. Limitations include fixed-backbone assumptions, overconfidence of structure predictors, lack of explicit joint landscape modeling, and limited large-scale experimental validation comparing these objective choices. Abstract: Designing protein sequences that reliably fold into a single intended structure requires accounting for both sequence compatibility with a backbone and the conformational landscape implied by that sequence. We propose a pipeline that jointly optimizes sequence-to-structure and structure-to-sequence models to explicitly model the coupled sequence-structure energy landscape during de novo design. The method alternates updates to sequence and backbone features using a structure predictor and an inverse-folding model, and combines model-specific likelihoods into hybrid scoring metrics that compare designs within the same fold. The primary contribution is a systematic pipeline and evaluation framework that quantitatively compares fixed-backbone design, structure-driven optimization, and joint optimization across large synthetic design sets. We expect joint optimization to produce sequences with higher empirical folding stability and better ranking by hybrid scores, and to reveal sequence-level features—such as increased hydrophilic pairwise contacts—that correlate with robustness. The pipeline enables objective comparisons of design objectives and provides a basis for improving predictive scoring functions for de novo protein stability. Experiments: Datasets: 1) Generate a corpus of 20,000 de novo mini-protein backbones with target lengths <= 80 residues using a structure-hallucination pipeline (structure predictor initialization with random sequences). 2) For each backbone, produce four designed sequences using: (A) structure-to-sequence model (ProteinMPNN), (B) sequence-to-structure optimization (TrRosetta/TrROS gradient-based sequence optimization), (C) joint optimization alternating TrROS and TrMRF updates, and (D) Rosetta design as an energy-based baseline. Retain at least 15,000 experimentally tractable sequences after filtering for cysteine-free and monomeric inter-PAE thresholds. Experimental measurement: measure folding stability (ΔG) for all retained sequences using a cDNA-display proteolysis assay and report per-sequence ΔG and protease resistance. Baselines: ProteinMPNN, TrROS, TrMRF (fixed-backbone), Rosetta energy score, AlphaFold2 pLDDT, ESMFold pLDDT, ESM-2 pseudo-likelihood. Metrics: Spearman and Pearson correlation between model scores and ΔG; AUROC and AUPRC for classifying stable (ΔG>5 kcal/mol) vs unstable (ΔG<0 kcal/mol); median ΔG per method; fraction of designs with alternative low-energy conformations assessed by structure prediction ensemble (RMSD clustering and alternative-state frequency); sequence diversity (pairwise identity), contact log-odds enrichment, and per-residue burial statistics. Experimental setup: randomize sequence-to-assay mapping in replicates (n>=3 technical replicates per sequence), blind assay operators to design method. Computational scoring: compute hybrid scores combining ProteinMPNN CCE and ESM-2 pseudo-likelihood with half-masked ESMFold pLDDT per provided convex weights; compare variants of hybrid weights in ablation. Ablations and comparisons: 1) Ablate sequence term from joint optimization (optimize only P(structure|sequence) with backbone updates) and ablate structure term (optimize only P(sequence|structure) while updating backbone). 2) Compare fixed-backbone ProteinMPNN designs filtered by AF2 pLDDT>85 to joint designs with same pLDDT filter. 3) Evaluate masking strategies for AF2/ESMFold (no masking, half-masking, full masking) and number of recycle steps on correlation to ΔG. Statistical analysis: compute bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for correlations and medians, apply paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for per-backbone ΔG differences between methods, and control for multiple comparisons using Benjamini-Hochberg FDR. Success criteria: joint method yields a statistically significant higher median ΔG and higher within-backbone Spearman correlation of hybrid score to ΔG than all single-objective baselines (p<0.01). Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: joint optimization may converge to adversarial sequences that exploit correlated biases in the structure and sequence models, producing high model scores but low experimental stability; gradient propagation through discrete sequence spaces may produce optimization artifacts. Model biases: structure predictors (AF2/ESMFold/TrROS) can be overconfident on non-native or out-of-distribution sequences, undermining score reliability; language-model pseudo-likelihoods may not reflect biophysical stability for de novo folds. Experimental biases: cDNA-display proteolysis measures protease resistance as a proxy for folding stability and may not capture all forms of misfolding, aggregation, or in vivo stability; assays may produce false signals from oligomerization or protease shielding. Data limitations: pipeline validated on mini-proteins (<80 aa) may not generalize to larger, multi-domain proteins or membrane proteins. Scalability and compute: joint iterative optimization and ensemble structure prediction require substantial compute and may be infeasible at proteome scale. Statistical risks: heterogeneity across folds may confound aggregated metrics; within-fold comparisons reduce but do not eliminate structural bias. Reproducibility: dependence on model checkpoints and hyperparameters can affect outcomes and impede reproducibility across different model versions.
